title: What this case is
html:
What this case is

Bobby Bronner was three days from becoming a citizen when the government moved him from an ordinary federal prosecution into offshore military detention.

Start with the procedural shift. The government sees a suspected terrorism case that justified military custody. Bronner sees a lawful resident removed from a functioning criminal court on sealed evidence. The disputed classification and process remain central. This guide abbreviates the record as R.

R. 4, 5 n.1 Bobby Bronner came to the United States at fifteen, fleeing a country where his mother had been placed under house arrest for a lecture criticizing its leader. He built a construction business, married an American, raised two American children, paid taxes, got a green card. In February 2025 the government formally approved his naturalization, expressly finding good moral character. He was scheduled to take the oath on July 4, 2025.

R. 4–5 An anonymous tipster called the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI). Rather than seek a warrant, agents bought four Ring cameras at a hardware store and mounted them on utility poles outside his house. They recorded for 93 straight days. On that footage the government got warrants; it found fentanyl in his home and car, and, at a warehouse, sealed documents it says show he arranged to buy a radiological "dirty bomb." He was arrested and arraigned in federal court, where he pleaded not guilty and was released on bond. The government immediately arrested him again, reclassified him through the Attorney General, transferred him to military control, and flew him to Guantanamo Bay on July 7, 2025. That transfer occurred three days after the citizenship oath he had been scheduled to take.

He has been there twelve months. He has never seen the evidence against him. R. 8

Posture — who won where

CourtFourth AmendmentArticle IIResult

Supreme CourtBronner is Petitioner; the United States is Respondent. Everything is reviewed de novo.
Naming trap

DeNolf is the President in this case, not the defendant. William DeNolf signed Executive Order 15,000 and personally ordered Bronner's transfer to military custody. The American Moot Court Association (AMCA) drafters recycled names and the state of Olympus from other problem sets — when you see "DeNolf," read "the government."

The cover page also carries the circuit-level labels ("Petitioner-Appellee," "Respondent-Appellant"). At the Supreme Court those flip: Bronner petitions, the United States responds.

What is not before the Court

Footnotes 8 and 9 of the majority opinion wall off entire lines of attack. These are as important as anything in the opinion:

  • The government did not argue it had probable cause independent of the pole-camera footage. R. 9 n.8
  • Bronner did not argue that Magistrate Judge Olson's warrant lacked probable cause. R. 9 n.8
  • No speedy-trial claim, no bail claim, no claim about introducing exculpatory evidence. R. 9 n.9
  • No treaties, protocols, or international agreements other than those in the appendices. R. 9 n.9
  • Jurisdiction is stipulated — nobody is litigating whether a Guantanamo detainee can seek habeas here. R. 9
  • All facts are stipulated; every issue is purely legal, reviewed de novo. R. 2

title: Timeline
html:
The timeline

Read each entry in date order. The February dates compare the President's order with the naturalization approval. The July dates compare the missed citizenship oath with the offshore transfer. The record's 93-day statement conflicts with the March 18 to May 27 arithmetic, so the guide preserves the stipulation and flags the conflict.

The highlighted dates show when one government decision followed another. Those short gaps test whether the government treated Bronner consistently and whether Congress had already addressed the detention power the President claimed.

  • 1995Bronner, 15, and his mother flee Sommerland after her house arrest. The U.S. embassy shelters them; they enter lawfully. R. 4, 5 n.1
  • Sept 2001Congress enacts the Authorization for Use of Military Force (AUMF). It authorizes "all necessary and appropriate force" against those responsible for September 11 and those who harbored them. R. 2; Appendix (App.) I (R. 20)
  • 2010Bronner obtains a green card at 30 after marrying a U.S. citizen. R. 4
  • Dec 31, 2011National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2012 (NDAA FY2012), Public Law (P.L.) 112-81, signed, §§ 1021–1022. Senate efforts to bar indefinite detention of Americans had already failed. R. 2–3
  • 2023 & 2025The Senate votes to repeal the AUMF. The House never takes it up. The AUMF stands. R. 3
  • Early 2024Bronner applies for naturalization. R. 4
  • Early 2025Congress enacts the Anti-Terrorist Act (ATA) after publicized violent crimes involving non-citizens. R. 3
  • Feb 14, 2025President DeNolf signs Executive Order (EO) 15,000, "Protection Against Terrorism" (PAT). PAT is a fictional executive order in this record, not the USA PATRIOT Act. R. 3–4; App. VI (R. 25)
  • Feb 17, 2025First hinge. United States Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) approves Bronner's naturalization after finding continuous residence and good moral character. The approval comes three days after the executive order later used against him. R. 4
  • Mar 17, 2025Anonymous tip from "Jersey": fentanyl importing, odd-hours visitors. Identity never discovered; source of her data unknown. R. 4
  • Mar 18, 2025Agents Bello and Cruz install four Ring cameras on utility poles on public property without a warrant. They customize retention to 180 days. This date begins the period that the record repeatedly calls 93 consecutive days of 24-hour motion-activated recording, even though the May 27 warrant date creates an arithmetic conflict. R. 4–5, 5 nn.3–4
  • May 4, 2025Roper and Langbourne visit Bronner for fifteen minutes. Both are foreign nationals with foreign convictions for selling military-grade arms. Bronner opens the door but never steps outside. R. 7
  • May 27, 2025National Security Agency (NSA) agents independently observe a warehouse meeting and decline to explain why they were watching. Assistant United States Attorney (AUSA) DeLeon wakes Magistrate Judge Olson; warrants issue. Parties stipulate the government relied primarily on the pole-camera footage. R. 7
  • May 29, 2025Agents search Bronner's property and find fentanyl patches, lollipops, spray, and a sales log. They find four boxes of lozenges in his car. The warehouse contains no drugs, but it does contain sealed documents that the government connects to a dirty bomb. Bronner is booked. R. 7–8
  • May 30, 2025Arraigned in an Article III court. Pleads not guilty. Released on bond. Immediately re-arrested for material support of a foreign terrorist organization. R. 8, 8 n.7
  • May 31, 2025Attorney General (AG) Comerford invokes PAT and ATA, classifying Bronner a "removable non-citizen with a criminal record" because he had been "accused." He has no convictions. R. 8
  • Jul 4, 2025Second hinge, scheduled citizenship: The scheduled oath of allegiance. It does not happen. R. 4
  • Jul 7, 2025Second hinge, military transfer: Surrendered to military authorities; flown to Guantanamo; placed in a high-security compound. R. 8
  • May 1, 2026Twelve months detained, uncharged in military custody, evidence sealed. Fourteenth Circuit reverses. R. 1, 8
A record wrinkle to know about

Cameras went up March 18 R. 5; the warrant issued May 27 R. 7 — 70 days, not 93. The record states 93 days three times, and both opinions accept that number. Use 93 days because it is stipulated. The March 18 to May 27 period is 70 days, but that arithmetic conflict does not change the legal question.

Record map — what is on every page

The record uses two page-numbering systems. This guide uses the PDF page and marks it as Record (R.). It identifies an appendix as App. before the appendix number, as in App. III (R. 21).

Use this map to locate each proposition. The parties draw different legal conclusions from the same stipulated pages, and the record contains four numbering or drafting inconsistencies.

Which page number does "R." mean? Verify this before you file anything

The case file carries two numbering systems, offset by one. Every page after the cover has a printed number in its top corner — but the cover page itself is unnumbered, so the printed number is always one lower than the PDF page. Printed "6" is PDF page 7.

This guide uses PDF page numbers, because the record itself does. The dissent cites "R. at 7" for the mosaic-theory facts, and those facts — the pizza deliveries, the Tuesday water jugs, the twice-weekly masseuse — sit on PDF page 7 (printed page 6). If the drafters had meant printed pages, that cite would point at the arrest-and-detention section, which has nothing to do with the mosaic theory.

That said, it is one internal cite. Confirm the convention against the AMCA rules or your coach before a brief is due, and if you need to hedge in writing, give both: "R. 7 (printed p. 6)."

title: The statutes, decoded
html:
The statutes, decoded

Question 2 first asks what Congress authorized. The constitutional category depends on that answer, so read each provision in plain language before assigning a Youngstown label.

Ask whom each provision covers, what custody it authorizes or requires, and what it leaves unresolved. The government reads the provisions together as support for detention. Bronner reads their limits and omissions as evidence that Congress withheld this specific power.

Public Law 107-40 (2001) · Appendix IR. 20; discussed R. 2, 13

Authorization for Use of Military Force (AUMF)

What it says
§ 2(a): the President may use all necessary and appropriate force against nations, organizations, or persons he determines planned, authorized, committed, or aided the 9/11 attacks, or harbored them, to prevent future acts of international terrorism by such nations, organizations, or persons.
What matters about the wording
Two limits are built in. First, it is tied to 9/11 and its perpetrators — the "by such" clause loops the prevention purpose back to the same actors. Second, "he determines" hands the identification to the President. Both sides use the same sentence: the government for the breadth of "all necessary and appropriate force," Bronner for the narrowness of who it reaches.
Status
Still in force. The Senate voted to repeal it in 2023 and 2025; the House never took the matter up. R. 3
10 U.S.C. § 948(a)(7) · Appendix IIR. 20; discussed R. 12

"Unprivileged enemy belligerent" — the definition

What it says
An individual who (A) has engaged in hostilities against the U.S. or its coalition partners; (B) has purposefully and materially supported such hostilities; (C) was part of al Qaeda at the time of the alleged offense; or (D) was previously defined as an "enemy combatant."
Why it matters
This is the label that unlocks detention without trial and trial by military commission. Note it is a definition in a chapter about military commissions, not itself a grant of detention power. And note prong (B) is the only one the government's theory can plausibly reach here.
P.L. 112-81 § 1021 · Appendix IIIR. 21; discussed R. 2–3, 13, 17

National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) § 1021, the affirmation of detention authority

(a) In general
Congress affirms that the President's AUMF authority includes the authority to detain "covered persons" pending disposition under the law of war. Note the verb: affirms, not grants. Congress is describing power it believes already exists.
(b) Covered persons
(1) those responsible for 9/11 or who harbored them; (2) a person who was part of or substantially supported al-Qaeda, the Taliban, or associated forces engaged in hostilities against the U.S., including anyone who committed a belligerent act or directly supported such hostilities in aid of such enemy forces.
This is the tightest textual constraint in the whole statutory scheme. § 1021 does not reach terrorism generally. It reaches al-Qaeda, the Taliban, and associated forces.
(c)(1) Disposition
Detention under the law of war without trial until the end of the hostilities authorized by the AUMF. The AUMF is therefore not just the source of the power — it is the clock.
(d) and (e) — the neutrality clauses
(d): nothing in this section is intended to limit or expand the President's authority or the AUMF's scope. (e): nothing shall be construed to affect existing law relating to detention of citizens, lawful resident aliens, or others captured or arrested in the United States.
These clauses are why the section is so hard to argue about. They deliberately freeze the pre-existing state of the law rather than resolving it — which means § 1021 can be read as confirming a power or as declining to create one.
P.L. 112-81 § 1022 · Appendix IVR. 22; discussed R. 2–3, 17–18

NDAA § 1022, military custody and the people carved out

(a) The requirement
The armed forces shall hold certain captured persons in military custody. Applies to those (A) part of al-Qaeda or an associated force acting in coordination with it, and (B) who participated in planning or carrying out an attack on the U.S. Note the conjunctive "and" — both prongs required.
(a)(4) Waiver
The President may waive the requirement by certifying to Congress in writing that waiver is in the national security interest.
(b) The carve-outs — the crux of the statutory fight
(1) "The requirement to detain a person in military custody under this section does not extend to citizens of the United States." (2) The same for lawful resident aliens, for conduct within the United States, "except to the extent permitted by the Constitution."
The government's reading: these lift an obligation, not a power. Congress said the military need not take these people; it did not say it may not.
Bronner's reading: Congress deliberately singled out citizens and lawful residents for protective treatment. Read with § 1021(e)'s preservation clause, Congress declined to expand authority over exactly this group.
Both readings are textually available. This is one of the genuinely unsettled points in the problem, not a place where one side is obviously right.
P.L. 417-01 (2025) · Appendix VR. 23–24; discussed R. 3, 14, 18

Anti-Terrorist Act (ATA) § 4 detention provisions

§ 4(a)
The Attorney General may direct the Department of Justice (DOJ) to detain any person present in the United States suspected of terrorism. No location specified.
§ 4(b)(1) — the offshore provision
DOJ may detain persons unlawfully present who are suspected of terrorism, conspiracy, or assistance. Such detention shall occur inside the U.S. — or outside, if the President expressly orders it upon finding the detainee would be at risk or a risk to others if held inside.
§ 4(b)(2) — citizens
Citizens may be detained, but must be held inside the territorial jurisdiction. No offshore authority for citizens at all.
The gap
The Act says nothing about lawfully present non-citizens — Bronner's category. It writes express rules for the unlawfully present (offshore permitted) and citizens (offshore forbidden) and leaves the middle blank.
What the record adds about that gap
In 2025 and 2026 both houses considered and rejected provisions allowing offshore detention of citizens. In 2026 the House passed a bill allowing offshore detention of lawfully present non-citizens with no criminal record — and it is still pending in the Senate. R. 3
What § 4 omits
No fixed time limit. No required finding of individualized dangerousness. No guaranteed access to counsel. No judicial review provision. R. 3
95 Fed. Reg. (Feb. 14, 2025) · Appendix VIR. 25; discussed R. 3–4

Executive Order 15,000, "Protection Against Terrorism" (PAT)

What it orders, and what PAT means here
PAT is the fictional Protection Against Terrorism executive order in this case file. It is not the USA PATRIOT Act. The Attorney General shall identify, remove, and detain outside the continental United States all non-citizens with criminal records or pending criminal charges whose presence the AG deems detrimental to national security — regardless of immigration status or length of residence. Guantanamo is named as an appropriate site.
The authorities it invokes
The ATA, the AUMF, "Congress's longstanding acquiescence in executive detention during national security emergencies," and inherent Article II authority. Section 3 adds: implemented "consistent with applicable law."
What the President said at signing
That in an evolving national-security threat, inherent foreign affairs and war powers allow the President to act beyond any specific law or statutory framework. That sentence R. 3–4 is the single most quotable line in the record for the argument that this is a Category 3 case: it is the executive claiming power independent of, and if necessary against, statute.
How it was applied to Bronner
The AG classified him as a non-citizen "with a criminal record" because he had been accused of a federal crime. He had no convictions. He did have pending charges, which the order separately covers — so the classification may reach the right result through the wrong words. R. 8

title: How the court below reasoned
html:
How the Fourteenth Circuit reasoned

The majority and dissent accept the same stipulated facts. They disagree about what those facts mean under the Fourth Amendment and Article II.

For each issue, the majority's reasoning comes first and the dissent's response follows. Question 1 asks whether aggregation changes public observation into a search. Question 2 asks whether Congress authorized, preserved, or opposed this offshore detention.

Question 1 — the majority's chain (Judge Barnhart)

  1. Start with Katz. Bronner must show that he actually expected privacy and that society recognizes that expectation as reasonable.
  2. No reasonable expectation in who enters and exits. Society doesn't protect what is readily observable from public vantage points. Cites Ciraolo. The cameras were on public poles; the driveway, front steps, and porch were street-visible; interior "observations" (lights, movement) existed only because Bronner left his blinds open.
  3. Answer duration in one sentence. "Duration alone does not transform lawful observation into a search," citing Tuggle at 526.
  4. Distinguish Kyllo on general public use. Motion tracking, zoom, and infrared are features of technology regularly used by the public for home security. Standalone devices, no network. They revealed no intimate details, penetrated no walls, and recorded only what was observable publicly.
  5. Distinguish Carpenter on scale and technology. 93 days from fixed vantage points versus ~13,000 location points; narrow targeting of an existing person of interest, not a dragnet; cell phones raise specialized concerns that a store-bought camera doesn't.
  6. Fallback: even if a search, it was reasonable. Minimal, passive intrusion against interests of the highest order — fentanyl trafficking and suspected domestic terror.

Question 1 — the dissent's chain (Judge Cassidy)

  1. Concede the premise, deny the conclusion. Public visibility is "correct as far as it goes" and does not resolve the case.
  2. Reframe Carpenter. What mattered was not the visibility of isolated movements but the government's ability to assemble a comprehensive chronicle. The majority treats Carpenter as a case about digital fishing; it is a case about aggregation.
  3. Invoke the mosaic idea explicitly, citing Tuggle's own survey of justices, judges, and scholars who have embraced it.
  4. Apply Kyllo more broadly. Even commonplace technology can reveal detailed domestic information when deployed persistently and in a targeted way. The features in combination — motion tracking, 10x zoom, infrared, persistent recording — allowed monitoring in conditions that defeat ordinary human observation.
  5. Use Kyllo's "all details are intimate details." The Court has refused to distinguish intimate from unimportant details of the home.
  6. Deploy Tafoya's holding sentence: duration, continuity, and nature of surveillance matter.
  7. The warrant point. No exigency, ample opportunity, and a magistrate reachable at night. The failure to seek one is fatal, citing Keith.
Where they genuinely disagree

Not about facts. About what the unit of analysis is. The majority asks whether each thing the cameras saw was private. The dissent asks whether the thing the government built was private. Everything else follows from that choice, and no case in the table of authorities squarely resolves it.

Question 2 — the majority's chain

  1. Start with the label. Bronner is an unprivileged enemy belligerent under 10 U.S.C. § 948(a)(7) because arranging to buy a dirty bomb from dealers investigated for terrorist ties is material support of hostilities.
  2. Inherent power exists. Prize Cases: the President need not wait for Congress to "baptize it with a name." Quirin: detention is a fundamental incident of waging war, and citizenship does not exempt an unlawful belligerent.
  3. But rest primarily on Congress. Authorization for Use of Military Force (AUMF) + National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) § 1021(b)(2) and (c)(1) + the Anti-Terrorist Act (ATA). Hamdi read the AUMF to include detention for the duration of hostilities.
  4. Add acquiescence. Failed amendments, failed repeals, a signing statement asserting the power, and Costanzo for the proposition that legislative inaction can create a presumption favoring a longstanding executive interpretation.
  5. Place it in Youngstown Category 1. Power at its maximum.
  6. Distinguish Milligan. Milligan was a civilian not supporting enemy forces, tried where courts were open; Quirin and Hamdi allow treating supporters of enemy forces as belligerents even if citizens and even if captured on U.S. soil.
  7. Due process is satisfied. Habeas is available and working. Detention is tied to hostilities and a plan to prosecute, not punishment. No six-month ceiling exists; no individualized determination is required absent evidence of a "ruse" (Banyee).

Question 2 — the dissent's chain

  1. Open with Hamdi's warning: a state of war is not a blank check — and extend it to lawful permanent residents.
  2. Reject Category 1. § 1022(b)(1)–(2) expressly declines to extend the military-custody requirement to citizens and lawful residents; § 1021(e) preserves existing law. Congress declined to impose the requirement and took care not to expand authority.
  3. Inaction is not a grant. Youngstown counsels caution where Congress has legislated and declined to confer the claimed power.
  4. Find Category 3. § 1022 plus ATA § 4(b)(2)'s inside-the-U.S. rule for citizens implies Congress rejected a presidentially created category of indefinite Guantanamo detainees. Lowest ebb.
  5. Narrow Quirin and Hamdi. Quirin: saboteurs sent by a foreign nation during a declared war, and the Court took pains to distinguish Milligan. Hamdi: tied to individuals captured in active combat zones. Bronner was living openly, arrested by civilian police, arraigned in federal court, held where civilian courts function.
  6. Distinguish the Prize Cases on the nature of the conflict. An active civil war between organized forces, not long-term detention far from any battlefield. The "War on Terror" is a never-ending concept, and that difference heightens the concern.
  7. Milligan controls the structure. The executive may not substitute military jurisdiction where civilian courts remain open and capable.
  8. Apply Mathews to the detention. Liberty from restraint at Guantanamo after twelve months is among the most significant interests the law recognizes; the risk of error is demonstrated by his arraignment and release on bond; the government hasn't shown why a neutral tribunal cannot test the classification.
  9. Offer a remedy. Banyee shows courts can require periodic review to keep authorized detention from becoming effectively indefinite.

title: The word "search"
html:
The Fourth Amendment turns on one word: search

The government defines the observed information one visible event at a time. Bronner defines it as a retained 93-day account of life at a home. Supreme Court cases support parts of both descriptions but do not decide this camera practice.

The text: "The right of the people to be secure in their persons, houses, papers, and effects, against unreasonable searches and seizures, shall not be violated..."

The warrant question begins only if the camera monitoring was a Fourth Amendment search. If it was not a search, the Amendment does not require a warrant or a reasonableness inquiry.

In ordinary speech, a search often means examining a bag or room to find what is inside. Fourth Amendment law does not require physical entry.

In Fourth Amendment law, observation can qualify as a search. The question is whether the government learned information that Bronner was entitled to keep private. No agent entered his land, but prolonged watching may still trigger constitutional protection.

Terms that mislead on their face
"Search"
Sounds like rummaging. Requires no touching, no entering. Pure looking can be a search.
"Reasonable expectation of privacy"
The phrase contains both a personal and a legal question. The half that decides cases is whether society will protect the expectation — a rule-for-everyone judgment. When a judge presses you on "expectation," they nearly always mean the second half.
"Curtilage"
Curtilage is the area immediately surrounding a home, including a porch, steps, or enclosed yard. Legally treated as part of the home. It decides Tafoya and it is where Bronner's facts are weakest.
"In general public use"
Kyllo's limiting phrase. Sounds like a simple factual question about who owns the gadget. It carries substantial constitutional weight. The government emphasizes that roughly 30% of U.S. homes have a doorbell camera.
"Plain view" / "public vantage point"
Public exposure matters, but it does not create an absolute rule that anything visible is fair game. Carpenter says so expressly: a person does not surrender all Fourth Amendment protection by venturing into public.
"Mosaic theory"
The mosaic theory is not a formally adopted Supreme Court doctrine. It describes the argument that many observations can reveal more than each observation considered alone. The Supreme Court has never adopted it by name and has never required lower courts to apply it — Tuggle says exactly that, and surveys courts that have rejected it as unworkable. Use the idea; don't call it settled.
"Case of first impression"
Only means: this court hasn't decided this exact question before. It signals that you should argue from principle, not from a controlling case.
"De novo"
"Fresh." The Supreme Court owes the Fourteenth Circuit no deference.

The Katz two-step — the frame everything sits inside

  1. Did the person actually expect privacy? (Subjective — did he behave as though this was private?)
  2. Is society prepared to call that expectation reasonable? (Objective.)

Step one is rarely where cases turn. Step two is the fight, every time. Note a subtlety Ciraolo adds: the test of legitimacy is not whether the individual chose to conceal something, but whether the government's intrusion infringes the values the Amendment protects.

Name the competing situations, not the labels

Situation A · the government's picture

The neighbor who happens to see

You leave your blinds up. The woman across the street notices the pizza guy at seven, notices two men in an SUV on Sunday, notices your porch light. She's on the sidewalk. Nobody thinks she needs a warrant.

Situation B · Bronner's picture

The lodger who never leaves

Someone rents the room across the street, sits at the window every hour of every day for three months, timestamps every arrival and departure, keeps a notebook they can reread for six months, and never sleeps — because they aren't a person.

The single question that resolves Question 1

Did the surveillance capture moments anyone could have seen — or did it assemble a picture no one could have seen?

This is the actual dividing line between the majority and the dissent, between Tuggle and Tafoya, and between Judge Lynch and Chief Judge Barron in Moore-Bush. The answer determines how the remaining Fourth Amendment rules apply to these facts.

Kind versus quantity — the distinction to keep straight

The government's framing is quantity: 93 days is a lot of days, and a lot of lawful looking is still lawful looking. Bronner's framing is kind: continuous automated recording, retained and searchable, is a different thing from observation — the way a transcript is a different thing from overhearing.

The reason this matters for understanding, not just advocacy: the quantity framing has no stopping point, and every court that adopts it says so. Tuggle upheld eighteen months while calling it "concerning." The Sixth Circuit upheld ten weeks. Courts that adopt the kind framing (Tafoya, Barron in Moore-Bush) don't need a number.

title: How the doctrine got here
html:
How the doctrine got here

Read chronologically, these nine cases show the doctrine moving from physical intrusion to privacy, technology, aggregation, and prolonged camera monitoring.

Each case adds a limit. Public exposure generally weakens privacy, but the home, uncommon technology, long duration, and aggregated records can strengthen it. The parties dispute which features control here.

  1. 1967 — Katz breaks the tie to property. Before Katz, the question was roughly whether the government trespassed. Katz says the Amendment protects people, not places, and a man in a glass phone booth can be searched by a microphone taped to the outside. What you knowingly expose to the public isn't protected; what you seek to preserve as private may be, even in a public place.
  2. 1972 — Keith says national security is not an exception. The government claimed the President's duty to protect against subversion allowed warrantless domestic wiretaps. The Court refused. Its reasoning is structural: the executive cannot be the neutral magistrate, because its job is to investigate and prosecute. Prior judicial approval is the check.
  3. 1986 — Ciraolo builds the "public vantage point" idea. Police flew a plane at 1,000 feet over a doubly-fenced backyard and saw marijuana with the naked eye. Not a search. The key words in the opinion are naked eye and public navigable airspace — anyone flying there who glanced down would have seen the same thing.
  4. 2001 — Kyllo draws a line at the wall. Thermal imaging of a home from a car across the street. Search. The rule: sense-enhancing technology not in general public use, used to obtain information about a home's interior that couldn't be had without physical intrusion. And critically, Scalia refuses to sort details by importance: all details of the home are intimate details.
  5. 2012 — Jones splits the Court three ways and plants the aggregation seed. GPS on a car for 28 days. The majority decides it on old-fashioned trespass — agents physically attached a device to an "effect." But five Justices across two concurrences say the real problem is duration. Alito (with Ginsburg, Breyer, Kagan): short-term monitoring is fine, but longer-term monitoring impinges on privacy, and "the line was surely crossed before the 4-week mark." Sotomayor adds the structural insight: this kind of surveillance is cheap and surreptitious, so it evades the two things that have always constrained police — limited resources and community hostility.
  6. 2018 — Carpenter makes aggregation the holding. 12,898 cell-site location points over 127 days. Search. The Court explicitly rejects the argument that public exposure of each movement defeats protection. It holds that accessing at least seven days of such records is a search and expressly reserves whether less would be. But it also inserts a limiting sentence that matters enormously here — see the caution box below.
  7. 2021 — Tuggle applies all of it to pole cameras and finds no search. Eighteen months, three cameras. The Seventh Circuit surveys the mosaic theory, notes the Supreme Court has never required lower courts to use it, and holds that these cameras captured only a "sliver" — not where Tuggle went, whom he met in public, or whose homes he visited. It reads Carpenter narrowly, as limited to historical location records that let the government travel back in time through a pre-existing database.
  8. 2021 — Tafoya goes the other way on fenced curtilage. Three months, a camera that could pan/tilt/zoom, footage stored indefinitely, capturing a backyard hidden by a six-foot privacy fence. Search. Colorado's holding sentence: duration, continuity, and nature of surveillance matter.
  9. 2022 — Moore-Bush shows the split is inside a single court. Eight months of pole-camera surveillance of front curtilage. The First Circuit sitting en banc unanimously reversed the suppression order — but for opposite reasons. Three judges said it was a search and reversed only on good faith; three said it was not a search at all.
The sentence in Carpenter that the government will build on

Carpenter says the Court was not "call[ing] into question conventional surveillance techniques and tools, such as security cameras." Tuggle seizes on it: whether pole cameras are technically the same as security cameras is beside the point, because they plainly qualify as a conventional surveillance tool.

This is the strongest single line in the entire Fourth Amendment material for the government, and it is not in the Fourteenth Circuit's opinion. Know it exists.

The passage in Tuggle that cuts hard the other way

Tuggle expressly rejects the Sixth Circuit's reasoning in Houston that surveillance is constitutional whenever police could theoretically have done it without technology. Tuggle calls that a fiction that "contravenes the Fourth Amendment and Katz's command to assess reasonableness," and says assuming the government could station agents on three telephone poles for eighteen months "defies the reasonable limits of human nature and finite resources."

So the leading case for the government destroys the "a passerby could have seen it" move that the Fourteenth Circuit majority leans on. Tuggle also closes by saying it is "not without unease" and calls eighteen months "concerning, even if permissible."

title: The nine cases
html:
The Fourth Amendment cases in full

Each case is organized by its facts, holding, reasoning, rule, and application to Bronner. The government emphasizes public visibility and conventional cameras. Bronner emphasizes aggregation, the home, and the limits of human observation.

Do not treat a case name as a conclusion. Compare what the technology captured, where it pointed, how long it operated, and whether the court treated isolated views or the compiled record as the relevant object.

389 U.S. 347 (1967)In your files

Katz v. United States — the glass phone booth

What happened
FBI agents taped an electronic listening device to the outside of a public telephone booth and recorded Charles Katz transmitting illegal wagering information. No physical entry into the booth. The booth was glass — anyone could see him standing in it.
Held
A search. The government's activity violated the privacy on which Katz justifiably relied while using the booth, and it was unreasonable because no warrant was obtained.
The reasoning
The Court abandoned the requirement of physical trespass. The Fourth Amendment protects people, not places. The famous formulation is a pair: what a person knowingly exposes to the public — even in his own home or office — is not protected; but what he seeks to preserve as private, even in an area accessible to the public, may be constitutionally protected.
The rule it set
The two-step test actually comes from Justice Harlan's concurrence, not the majority: (1) a subjective expectation of privacy, (2) one society recognizes as reasonable. Everything in Question 1 runs through it.
Its role here
The shared frame. Both opinions below cite it in the first paragraph of their Fourth Amendment analysis. Note the structure of Katz's win: he was visible to everyone and still prevailed, because what he protected was not his image.
407 U.S. 297 (1972)In your files

United States v. United States District Court ("Keith") — domestic security is not a warrant exception

What happened
Three defendants were charged with conspiring to destroy government property; one with dynamiting a CIA office. The government admitted warrantless wiretaps, supported by an Attorney General affidavit stating the taps gathered intelligence "necessary to protect the nation from attempts of domestic organizations to attack and subvert the existing structure of the Government." It argued this was a reasonable exercise of presidential power.
Held
Two holdings. (1) Title III § 2511(3), which said nothing in the Act limits the President's power to protect against overthrow, is merely a disclaimer of congressional intent — not a grant of authority. (2) The Fourth Amendment requires prior judicial approval for domestic security surveillance of this type.
The reasoning — this is the part worth knowing
The Court's core move is institutional, not factual: "The Fourth Amendment does not contemplate the executive officers of Government as neutral and disinterested magistrates." Their duty is to enforce, investigate, and prosecute — so they should not be the sole judges of when to use constitutionally sensitive means. The historical judgment the Amendment accepts is that unreviewed executive discretion "may yield too readily to pressures to obtain incriminating evidence."
It also rejects the government's fallback that after-the-fact review suffices: post-surveillance review would never reach the surveillances that never result in prosecutions. And it concedes the surveillance here might well have been approved had a warrant been sought — which is precisely why one should have been.
The limit Keith drew around itself
The Court expressly reserved "the issues which may be involved with respect to activities of foreign powers or their agents." Keith is about domestic security. That reservation is the government's answer whenever Keith is cited in a case involving alleged foreign terrorist ties.
Its role here
The dissent's warrant argument, and the closest thing in the case file to a bridge between the two questions: the deference the government asks for on Article II is the deference Keith refused on the Fourth Amendment.
476 U.S. 207 (1986)In your files

California v. Ciraolo — the plane over the fence

What happened
An anonymous tip said marijuana was growing in a backyard shielded from ground-level view by two fences. Officers trained in marijuana identification chartered a private plane, flew over at 1,000 feet, and identified the plants with the naked eye. A photograph was attached to the warrant application as an exhibit.
Held
Not a search. 5–4, Burger, C.J. (Powell, J., dissenting, joined by Brennan, Marshall, Blackmun).
The reasoning
The Court accepted that the yard was curtilage and that Ciraolo had a subjective expectation of privacy — the fences established it. It lost on the second prong. Being within curtilage does not itself bar all police observation. Taking measures to restrict some views does not preclude observation from a public vantage point where the officer has a right to be and from which the activity is clearly visible. Any member of the public flying in that airspace who glanced down would have seen the same thing.
One line worth remembering: the test of legitimacy is not whether the individual chose to conceal private activity, but whether the government's intrusion infringes the personal and societal values the Amendment protects.
The rule it set
Lawful vantage point + naked eye + physically nonintrusive = no search, even of curtilage. It is the foundation of every "but it was visible from the street" argument.
Its limits — and how Moore-Bush explains them
Chief Judge Barron's opinion in Moore-Bush makes the sharpest point available about Ciraolo: it reasons about the "casual, accidental observer." Nobody has ever encountered a casual observer "who could take in all that occurs in a home's curtilage over the course of eight months and recall it perfectly and at a moment's notice." Ciraolo tells you what a glance means. It doesn't tell you what a ledger means.
Its role here
Cited by the majority for the public-vantage principle. Not in your table of authorities as an attached case in the original set — it is now.
533 U.S. 27 (2001)In your files

Kyllo v. United States — the thermal imager and the grow lamps

What happened
Agents suspected Danny Kyllo of growing marijuana indoors. From a car across the street they aimed a thermal imaging device at his triplex for a few minutes and saw that his garage wall and roof were unusually hot — consistent with high-intensity grow lamps. That reading supported a warrant.
Held
A search. Where the government uses sense-enhancing technology not in general public use to obtain information regarding the interior of the home that could not otherwise be obtained without physical intrusion, that is a search and is presumptively unreasonable without a warrant.
The reasoning
Scalia's concern was that technology "shrinks the realm of guaranteed privacy" — it lets the government get, from outside, what previously required going in. The Amendment must at minimum preserve the degree of privacy that existed when it was adopted.
He then refused the government's fallback that the device revealed only trivial information: "all details are intimate details, because the entire area is held safe from prying government eyes." The Court declined to make judges sort a home's contents into important and unimportant.
The rule it set — and its built-in weakness
Two conditions do the work: interior of the home, and not in general public use. The second is the one everyone fights about, because it means Fourth Amendment protection contracts as consumer technology spreads. That is a known and much-criticized feature of the rule, not an accident.
Its role here
Both opinions rely on it and read it in opposite directions. Majority: Ring cameras are in general public use and penetrated no walls. Dissent: the aggregate use of motion tracking, zoom, infrared, and persistent recording revealed information about domestic rhythms, and "all details are intimate details" forecloses calling that trivial.
565 U.S. 400 (2012)In your files

United States v. Jones — the GPS on the Jeep

What happened
The government got a warrant to install a GPS device on a vehicle registered to Antoine Jones's wife — authorized for the District of Columbia and within 10 days. Agents installed it on the 11th day, in Maryland, so the warrant was worthless. They then tracked the vehicle for 28 days.
Held
A search — unanimously in result, on three different theories.
The majority's reasoning (Scalia)
Decided on old ground. The government physically occupied private property — an "effect" — for the purpose of obtaining information. That would have been a search in 1791. Katz's expectation test was added to, not substituted for, the trespass test. The Court expressly declined to reach whether Jones had a reasonable expectation of privacy.
Alito's concurrence in the judgment (with Ginsburg, Breyer, Kagan)
Rejects the trespass approach as an accident of technology and asks whether the use of GPS "involved a degree of intrusion that a reasonable person would not have anticipated." His answer: short-term monitoring of public movements accords with reasonable expectations; longer-term monitoring in most investigations does not, because society's expectation is that agents "would not — and indeed, in the main, simply could not — secretly monitor and catalogue every single movement" for a very long period. "[T]he line was surely crossed before the 4-week mark." He declines to say where it is.
Sotomayor's concurrence — the most-borrowed passage in this entire area
She joins the majority but adds four structural points that Tafoya, Carpenter, and Barron in Moore-Bush all reuse: GPS generates a precise, comprehensive record reflecting familial, political, professional, religious, and sexual associations; the government can store and efficiently mine it years into the future; because it is cheap and surreptitious, it evades the ordinary checks that constrain abusive practices — "limited police resources and community hostility"; and awareness that the government may be watching chills associational and expressive freedom.
She also says she does not regard as dispositive that the government could have obtained the same fruits through conventional means — the exact point Tuggle later adopts.
Its role here
Not cited in the Fourteenth Circuit's opinions, but it is the source of nearly everything in them. If you want to understand why "duration" became a Fourth Amendment argument at all, this is where it starts.
585 U.S. 296 (2018)In your files

Carpenter v. United States — twelve thousand dots on a map

What happened
After a string of Radio Shack and T-Mobile robberies, the government obtained Timothy Carpenter's cell-site location information from his wireless carriers under the Stored Communications Act — a standard lower than probable cause. It received 12,898 location points across 127 days, about 101 per day.
Held
A search. Accessing at least seven days of historical cell-site location information (CSLI) requires a warrant. The Court expressly declined to decide whether a shorter period would.
The reasoning
Two threads converge. From the Jones concurrences: individuals have a reasonable expectation of privacy in the whole of their physical movements, and the government's ability to compile a comprehensive chronicle of a life is the harm. From the third-party doctrine cases: a person does not surrender all Fourth Amendment protection by venturing into the public sphere.
The Court emphasized CSLI's retrospective quality — it gives police access to a category of information "otherwise unknowable," letting them travel back in time to retrace someone's whereabouts. Previously, reconstructing a person's movements was limited by "a dearth of records and the frailties of recollection."
The self-imposed limits — read these carefully
Carpenter calls itself a narrow decision. It does not disturb conventional surveillance techniques and tools, "such as security cameras." It does not address real-time CSLI or tower dumps. Lower courts, including the Seventh Circuit in Hammond and then Tuggle, have used these caveats to confine it to historical location databases.
Its role here
The center of gravity for Question 1. The majority reads it as a case about a specialized device and enormous scale; the dissent reads it as a case about aggregation whose logic doesn't care what hardware produced the record.
4 F.4th 505 (7th Cir. 2021)In your files

United States v. Tuggle — eighteen months, and a court that didn't like its own answer

What happened
Investigating a methamphetamine conspiracy in central Illinois, agents installed three cameras on public utility poles around Travis Tuggle's home — two viewing the front of the house and adjoining parking area, one primarily viewing a co-defendant's shed. They recorded around the clock for roughly eighteen months (Aug. 2014 – Mar. 2016). Agents could remotely zoom, pan, and tilt and watch live; footage was stored at the FBI office. No infrared and no audio. The cameras captured over 100 suspected drug deliveries.
Held
Not a search. "The government's use of a technology in public use, while occupying a place it was lawfully entitled to be, to observe plainly visible happenings, did not run afoul of the Fourth Amendment."
The reasoning in five steps
1. The mosaic theory isn't binding. The court traces it from Maynard (D.C. Cir. 2010) through the Jones concurrences to Carpenter, notes that scholars say Carpenter "effectively endorsed" it, and then holds that the Supreme Court "has not yet required lower courts to apply it." Several courts have rejected it as unworkable because constitutionality would hinge on duration.
2. Even accepting it, these facts don't qualify. The cameras captured "an important sliver" of Tuggle's life but not "the type of exhaustive picture of his every movement" the Court has frowned upon. They exposed nothing about where he traveled, what businesses he frequented, whom he met in public, or whose homes he visited.
3. Carpenter is about retrospective databases. The government had to decide ex ante to install the cameras; it did not tap a pre-existing archive. So it could not "travel back in time." Carpenter is read as limited to historical CSLI.
4. Carpenter's own carve-out. The Court said it was not calling into question conventional tools "such as security cameras." Whether pole cameras are the same as security cameras is irrelevant — they are plainly conventional.
5. But the "could have done it manually" fiction is dead. The court expressly rejects the Sixth Circuit's Houston reasoning. Assuming the government could allocate thousands of hours to station agents atop three poles for eighteen months "defies the reasonable limits of human nature and finite resources." It "closes the door" on the idea that technological surveillance is constitutional simply because it could theoretically be done without technology.
What Tuggle says about itself
It opens with a page-long meditation on a coming world of ubiquitous cameras and observes that under Katz, evolving expectations "continually undermine themselves" — as the government moves discreetly with the times, its use of advanced technology never breaches society's reconstituted non-expectations. It closes saying it is "not without unease," calling eighteen months "concerning, even if permissible," and noting it decided as it did because it was bound by Supreme Court precedent and without other statutory or jurisprudential means to cabin the practice.
Its role here
The majority's authority for "duration alone does not transform." Understand what that citation is doing: it is a circuit court applying a theory it declined to adopt, reaching a result it said it disliked, and inviting Congress or the Supreme Court to fix it.
494 P.3d 613 (Colo. 2021)In your files

People v. Tafoya — the fence, the tire, and the $98,000

What happened
An informant told Colorado Springs police that Rafael Tafoya's house was a drug stash house. Police mounted a camera on a utility pole across the street — no warrant — that could pan, tilt, and zoom on command while officers watched live, and recorded continuously for over three months, with footage stored indefinitely. Because of its elevated angle it recorded a backyard enclosed by a six-foot wooden privacy fence with a gate. Officers watched Tafoya let a car through the gate, close it, and crouch at the front-left tire; men later carried a spare tire from the garage to a truck. Police stopped the truck and found $98,000 in the tire.
Held
A warrantless search in violation of the Fourth Amendment. Convictions reversed.
The reasoning
Prong one was easy: the area was curtilage, set back from the street, and fenced with a gate he closed. Subjective expectation established.
Prong two is the whole opinion. The court weighed public exposure against duration, continuity, and nature of the surveillance, and imported Sotomayor's four Jones factors nearly wholesale: it created a precise, comprehensive record of activities at the home; it was stored so the government could mine it years later; it was surreptitious — had an officer manned the pole for three months, Tafoya would obviously have noticed; and because it was cheap and surreptitious it evaded the ordinary checks of limited resources and community hostility.
On public exposure the court gave the sharpest available answer: exposure may diminish an expectation but is not determinative, quoting Carpenter and Katz. Tafoya's exposure was fleeting — a neighbor peering through fence gaps, or someone on an apartment stairway. Fleeting exposure does not equal continuous recording.
The holding sentence
"[T]he duration, continuity, and nature of surveillance matter when considering all the facts and circumstances in a particular case." The dissent below quotes exactly this.
Its role here and the factual limit
The only pole-camera decision favoring suppression among the cases cited. But Tafoya's facts are meaningfully better than Bronner's: the camera saw a fenced backyard invisible from the street, and the Colorado court repeatedly grounds its analysis in curtilage. Bronner's cameras captured a porch, steps, driveway, and door all visible from nearby streets. Anyone relying on Tafoya has to rely on its reasoning rather than its outcome — which is a real move, since duration/continuity/nature does not logically require a fence, but it is a move, not a given.
One more thing worth knowing
Tafoya explicitly distinguished Tuggle on this ground: in Tuggle, "the area surveilled was not curtilage or surrounded by a fence." Colorado thought the fence was doing work. That admission cuts against using Tafoya for Bronner.
36 F.4th 320 (1st Cir. 2022) (en banc)In your files

United States v. Moore-Bush — six judges, two answers, one result

What happened
ATF investigated Nia Moore-Bush for selling illegal firearms and trafficking heroin. A cooperating witness bought four guns at the house; a traffic stop recovered 921 bags of heroin. About a week later, agents installed a pole camera on a utility pole outside 120 Hadley Street, Springfield, Massachusetts. It showed the right side of the house, the attached garage, a side door, and the driveway — not the front door — and a tree partially obstructed the view much of the time. It recorded for eight months.
Procedural history — this is why the case is confusing
The district court (Judge Young) suppressed. A First Circuit panel reversed. The full court took it en banc and vacated the panel opinion. On rehearing, the en banc court issued a per curiam holding: the suppression order is unanimously reversed — followed by two three-judge concurrences that agree on nothing else.
Barron, C.J., with Thompson and Kayatta — it WAS a search
The government conducted a search when it accessed the digital record it created over eight months, notwithstanding that the record is a compendium of images of what was publicly exposed. Their key reasoning about Ciraolo: the government's fence argument treats the claimed expectation as if it concerned discrete occurrences, when the claim is about the totality over months. Failing to build a fence signals willingness to be casually observed. It says nothing about willingness to be compiled.
They nonetheless reversed, because circuit precedent (United States v. Bucci, 2009) had held nearly identical surveillance was not a search, so the good-faith exception applied. They would overrule Bucci going forward.
Lynch, Howard, and Gelpí — it was NOT a search
All the views were "totally exposed to public observation." They argue the Barron opinion misapplies Carpenter — that Carpenter forbids rather than supports it — and contradicts a fundamental doctrine recognized in Kyllo. They also stress the investigative record: the camera was "a well-elaborated and targeted use of limited government resources," and its duration "was dictated by the needs of the investigation."
Its role here
The majority below cites Lynch; the dissent cites Barron. It is the clearest available evidence that the question is unsettled — a full federal appellate court, on nearly these facts, divided evenly on the constitutional question while agreeing on the outcome.
Two more cases that appear inside these opinions

United States v. Knotts (1983) — a beeper in a chloroform container tracked a car on public roads. Not a search. Source of the line that police may use technology to "augment the sensory faculties bestowed upon them at birth." Both Tafoya and the trial court in Tafoya quote it.

United States v. Houston (6th Cir. 2016) — ten weeks of pole-camera surveillance of a farm. Not a search. Source of the reasoning that only the possibility that a member of the public may observe from a public vantage point matters, "not the actual practicability of law enforcement's doing so without technology." Tuggle expressly rejected this reasoning even while reaching the same result. If someone invokes the passerby fiction, Houston is where it comes from and Tuggle is where it dies.

title: The pole-camera split
html:
The pole-camera split, on one screen

The cases do not draw a settled duration rule. Outcomes track most closely whether the camera recorded fenced curtilage or only areas visible from public streets, although two nonbinding opinions break that pattern.

The table shows genuine uncertainty rather than a duration threshold. Federal appellate outcomes favor the government, while fenced curtilage and aggregation reasoning give Bronner his strongest support.
