Cuevas-Sanchez (5th Cir. 1987)2 monthsFenced curtilageYesYes
State v. Jones (S.D. 2017)2 monthsAll activities outside the home — despite being street-visibleNoYes
Bronner (14th Cir. 2026)93 daysPorch, steps, driveway, front door, windows; interior lights/movement; 10x zoom, infrared, pan; 180-day retentionSlat fence, but it did not obscure what was recordedNo (2–1)
What the table shows

Duration does not predict outcome. Eighteen months lost; two months won. Curtilage largely does — every case finding a search except State v. Jones and Barron's Moore-Bush opinion involved a fence or genuinely non-public area.

That pattern favors the government because his cameras recorded only areas the record concedes were street-visible. The two decisions that break the pattern — State v. Jones (street-visible activities, still a search) and Barron's Moore-Bush concurrence (no fence, still a search) — are therefore the two most important non-binding authorities in the entire Fourth Amendment material for his side.

title: Applied to Bronner
html:
Applied to Bronner — what each fact does

The facts are grouped by the inference each side draws. No single fact resolves the issue. Public visibility favors the government, while continuous recording, enhanced features, and retention favor Bronner.

Pushes toward "search"
  • 93 consecutive days, 24 hours a day, motion-activated recording. R. 5
  • Four cameras, not one. R. 4–5
  • 180-day retention — deliberately customized above the 30/60-day default. This is the fact that best supports the Tafoya/Sotomayor "stored and mineable" point. R. 5 n.4
  • Remote pan; 10x optical zoom, about twice a phone's; used to identify Roper and Langbourne on May 4. R. 5, 7
  • Infrared night vision — the only feature in the record that obtains information under conditions defeating ordinary observation. The closest thing to a Kyllo hook. R. 5
  • Recorded the front door and windows, and the physical characteristics of anyone entering or exiting. R. 5
  • Recorded interior lights going on and off and movement near windows in common areas. R. 6
  • Produced a pattern of life: pizza twice weekly, Sparklets Tuesdays, Blue Apron Thursdays, Chewy and Omaha Steaks monthly, Geek Squad, HVAC, Girl Scout cookies — and a masseuse twice a week. Twice-weekly in-home personal care is the single most Sotomayor-flavored fact in the record. R. 6; cited by dissent at R. 15
  • No warrant, no exigency, 93 days of opportunity — and a magistrate who proved reachable in the middle of the night. R. 5, 7
  • Stipulated: the government relied primarily on this footage for probable cause. R. 7
Pushes toward "not a search"
  • Cameras on public property; no agent entered or touched Bronner's property. R. 4–5
  • Porch, steps, driveway, front door visible from nearby streets. No gate on the driveway. House set well back from the street. R. 5
  • The slat fence obscured most of the property — but not what the cameras recorded. Unlike Tafoya, no hidden curtilage was captured. This is the government's best single fact. R. 5
  • Interior visibility existed only because Bronner chose to leave his blinds open most of the day. R. 6
  • Zoom could not see items inside the home or identify features of occupants inside. R. 6
  • Audio-capable but no intelligible statements ever recorded. R. 5 n.4
  • Standalone consumer devices — no network, no other Ring users, no Ring–police partnership, Search Party unused, Knerr PD not among Ring's ~200 partner departments out of ~19,000. R. 5 nn.5–6
  • Ring cameras in roughly 30% of U.S. homes; at least 10 million Ring units — the "general public use" answer to Kyllo. R. 5 n.3
  • Targeted at one existing person of interest following a tip; no dragnet. R. 4, 10
  • Nothing was learned about where Bronner went after leaving — the exact distinction Tuggle drew from Carpenter and Jones. R. 10–11
Current law and remaining uncertainty

Under current federal appellate law, the government's position is the majority position. Every federal circuit to reach the question has upheld warrantless pole cameras. Carpenter carved out security cameras by name. Tuggle rejected the mosaic theory as non-binding on facts three times longer than Bronner's.

What Bronner has is not precedent but reasoning: Sotomayor's four factors, Alito's four-week line, Barron's compilation point, Tafoya's duration/continuity/nature formula, Tuggle's own rejection of the passerby fiction, and Kyllo's refusal to sort intimate details from trivial ones. Understanding this case means understanding that the Supreme Court granting certiorari is itself the interesting fact — there is no circuit split to resolve except the one between the circuits and a state supreme court.

title: Who said he could
html:
Article II asks who authorized the detention

The government says Congress supported detention and Article II supplies additional power. Bronner says the statutes do not cover him and the President displaced an available civilian process. Youngstown supplies the framework, but statutory fit remains disputed.

In plain terms, the government must identify the legal source for moving Bronner from federal court to military detention. Article II gives the President "the executive Power," makes him "Commander in Chief of the Army and Navy," and requires him to "take Care that the Laws be faithfully executed." None of those phrases mentions imprisoning anyone. There is no operative word to unpack, and that absence is the problem.

The President may rely on authority Congress supplied or on power that Article II gives the office independently. The parties dispute both sources.

  1. Congress said he could. Then the fight is about statutory text.
  2. The office carries the power on its own, whether Congress spoke or not. Then the fight is about constitutional structure.

The government invokes both sources, and Bronner disputes both. The framework from Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer sorts the claim according to what Congress has said.

Terms that mislead on their face
"Zone of twilight" / "lowest ebb"
These phrases identify how much support a presidential act receives from Congress. The "zone of twilight" describes uncertain or overlapping authority. The "lowest ebb" describes action contrary to Congress.
"Unprivileged enemy belligerent"
The most important trap in the case. The phrase sounds like a factual description, but it is a legal classification with serious consequences. The government must show that Bronner meets the statutory definition; the Attorney General's decision to use the label does not prove that conclusion by itself. Bronner has not seen the sealed evidence used to classify him.
"Sole organ" (Curtiss-Wright)
The phrase does not make the President the whole federal government in foreign affairs. The broad language is dictum. Justice Jackson explained this in Youngstown footnote 2: Curtiss-Wright involved "not the question of the President's power to act without congressional authority, but the question of his right to act under and in accord with an Act of Congress," and "much of the Court's opinion is dictum."
"Congressional acquiescence"
The claim that Congress's silence ratifies executive practice. In Costanzo, where it comes from, it required a consistent departmental construction published in successive rulebooks over fifteen years, plus congressional failure to amend. Silence that points in two directions at once is not acquiescence.
"Due process"
Due process does not guarantee a favorable outcome. It requires a meaningful opportunity to learn the basis for the government's action and answer it before a neutral decision-maker. That procedural question is central here because Bronner cannot see the evidence used to justify military detention. The Fifth Amendment's word is "person," not "citizen."
"Lawful permanent resident"
A lawful permanent resident is a green-card holder whom the United States has admitted to live here permanently. Bronner had this status, and United States Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) had approved his naturalization, but he had not yet taken the oath required for citizenship.
"Habeas corpus"
Habeas corpus requires the government to justify why it is holding a person. It tests the legality of detention, not guilt on the criminal charge. Bronner can therefore challenge his military confinement even though no court has tried the detention allegations.
"Law of war detention"
Law-of-war detention allows the government to hold a captured fighter until the relevant hostilities end so that the fighter cannot return to battle. The government describes this as prevention rather than punishment, which is why it says no criminal trial is required. Bronner answers that a conflict with no clear endpoint could make that detention permanent.
Situation A · the government's picture

The soldier taken off the field

An armed fighter captured in a combat zone may be held until the fighting ends so that he cannot return to battle. The detention prevents a return to hostilities rather than punishing a completed crime. Hamdi recognized that authority for a person allegedly captured while fighting with the Taliban in Afghanistan.

Situation B · Bronner's picture

The defendant taken out of the courtroom

A man is arrested at his house by the FBI, arraigned before a federal judge, pleads not guilty, and is released on bond. An ordinary criminal case in an open court. Then the executive removes him from it.

The single question that resolves Question 2

Was this man taken off a battlefield, or taken out of a courtroom?

Because the record answers it. Bronner was arraigned in an Article III court and released on bond on May 30, and handed to the military on July 7. Civilian process was not unavailable. It was already running. Milligan limits military jurisdiction where civilian courts are open. Quirin and Hamdi involved people treated as enemy fighters during active hostilities, so the parties dispute which comparison controls. The whole of Question 2 is a fight about which of those three cases this most resembles.

title: The Youngstown categories
html:
The Youngstown categories, in Jackson's own reasoning

Justice Jackson's three categories measure presidential authority by comparing the President's action with Congress's position. His method for identifying that position matters as much as the labels.

First identify Congress's position, then assign a category. The government reads the Authorization for Use of Military Force (AUMF), National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), and Anti-Terrorist Act (ATA) as authorization or preservation. Bronner reads their coverage limits and rejected proposals as opposition. The neutral clauses make the classification contestable.

Category 1 · Congress said yes, expressly or impliedly

Power at its maximum

His authority "includes all that he possesses in his own right plus all that Congress can delegate." Only here may he be said to personify federal sovereignty. If the act is unconstitutional in this posture, it usually means the federal government as a whole lacks the power. Such an act carries "the strongest of presumptions and the widest latitude of judicial interpretation," and the burden rests heavily on the challenger.

Jackson's warning about this category: it is where "the broadest recent statements of presidential power" come from — including Curtiss-Wright — and those statements "must be confined to this category."

Category 2 · Congress is silent

The zone of twilight

He relies on his own independent powers, but he and Congress may have concurrent authority, or the distribution may simply be uncertain. Congressional "inertia, indifference or quiescence" may as a practical matter enable, if not invite, independent presidential action. Any test of power here "is likely to depend on the imperatives of events and contemporary imponderables rather than on abstract theories of law."

Category 3 · Congress said no, expressly or impliedly

Power at its lowest ebb

He may rely only on his own constitutional powers minus any constitutional powers of Congress over the matter. Courts can sustain exclusive presidential control "only by disabling the Congress from acting upon the subject." This is the "least favorable of possible constitutional postures."

How Jackson classified Truman's seizure

  1. Step 1. Category 1 did not apply. The government conceded that Congress had not authorized Truman's seizure. The broad precedents about presidential power backed by Congress therefore could not support him.
  2. Step 2. Category 2 did not apply either. Congress had not "left seizure of private property an open field." It had enacted three statutory policies inconsistent with this seizure. Truman used none of them. "In choosing a different and inconsistent way of his own, the President cannot claim that it is necessitated or invited by failure of Congress to legislate."
  3. Step 3. The seizure fell in Category 3. Because Truman chose a method inconsistent with Congress's policy, the Court could uphold it only if the Constitution placed steel-mill seizures beyond Congress's control.
Applying Jackson's method to Bronner

Jackson's step 2 is the template for Bronner's Category 3 argument, and it is exactly the shape of the ATA: Congress did not leave offshore detention an open field. It wrote express rules for the unlawfully present (offshore permitted on presidential finding) and for citizens (offshore forbidden), and rejected proposals in both 2025 and 2026 to extend the power further. The President chose a different way of his own.

The government's answer has to be that the ATA is not exhaustive — that § 4(c) ("nothing in this section is intended to limit or expand the authority of the President") keeps the field open, which puts this at worst in Category 2. Section 4(c) therefore gives the government a serious Category 2 argument, while the ATA's detailed treatment of other groups supports Bronner's Category 3 argument.

Three other parts of Jackson's reasoning that bear on Bronner

  • On the Commander in Chief clause: "these cryptic words have given rise to some of the most persistent controversies in our constitutional history." It puts the armed forces under presidential command. But no doctrine "would seem to me more sinister and alarming" than that a President can "vastly enlarge his mastery over the internal affairs of the country by his own commitment of the Nation's armed forces to some foreign venture." He has no monopoly of "war powers," whatever they are.
  • On inward versus outward force — the most directly useful passage: he would "indulge the widest latitude of interpretation to sustain his exclusive function to command the instruments of national force, at least when turned against the outside world for the security of our society. But when it is turned inward," it should have no such indulgence.
  • On the source of executive power generally: "the executive branch, like the Federal Government as a whole, possesses only delegated powers." He rejects reading the Vesting Clause as "a grant in bulk of all conceivable executive power."
The majority holding and the later framework

The Youngstown majority opinion (Justice Black) is short and formalist — the President's power must stem from an act of Congress or the Constitution, and lawmaking is Congress's job. Courts use Jackson's concurrence instead, and have for seventy years. When a judge asks "what did Youngstown hold," the accurate answer is that the holding was Black's and the framework is Jackson's.

title: The nine cases
html:
The Article II cases in full

These cases separate emergency response, congressional authorization, military detention, and the process owed to a detainee. The government relies on war powers and congressional support. Bronner relies on open civilian courts, statutory limits, and neutral review.

Read the war cases separately from the process cases. The government uses the former to establish detention authority. Bronner uses Milligan, Youngstown, Mathews, and Hamdi to demand statutory authorization and neutral review.

67 U.S. (2 Black) 635 (1863)In your files

The Prize Cases — Lincoln's blockade before Congress showed up

What happened
After Fort Sumter, and before Congress acted, Lincoln proclaimed a blockade of Southern ports. Navy ships seized merchant vessels as prizes. The owners sued, arguing there was no war because Congress had not declared one, so the seizures were unlawful.
Held
The seizures were lawful. The President may meet an armed rebellion without waiting for Congress to "baptize it with a name." A war forced upon the nation is a war whether or not declared.
The reasoning
The President has no power to initiate war, but when war is thrust upon the country he is bound to resist force by force. He does not initiate the war; he meets it, and the question of what degree of force the crisis demands is one he must decide.
What it establishes
Inherent presidential authority to respond to an attack in progress, and the principle that a state of war can exist as a matter of fact rather than declaration.
Its role here
The majority uses it for the proposition that detention is an incident of war and the principle applies to modern terrorism. The dissent narrows it on two grounds: it arose from open hostilities between organized forces, and it did not involve long-term detention of residents seized far from any battlefield. The dissent's deeper point is temporal — a blockade ends when a war ends, and the "War on Terror" is a never-ending concept.
71 U.S. (4 Wall.) 2 (1866)In your files

Ex parte Milligan — the civilian tried by soldiers in Indiana

What happened
Lambdin Milligan, an Indiana civilian and Confederate sympathizer, was arrested during the Civil War, tried by a military commission, and sentenced to hang for conspiring to free Confederate prisoners. Indiana was never a theater of war; its federal authority was never opposed and its courts were open and operating throughout.
Held
The military commission had no jurisdiction. Milligan was entitled to release.
The reasoning in four steps
1. The commission wasn't a court. It was not "ordained and established by Congress," and its members were not judges appointed during good behavior.
2. The President can't create one. He "is controlled by law, and has his appropriate sphere of duty, which is to execute, not to make, the laws." There is "no unwritten criminal code to which resort can be had as a source of jurisdiction."
3. The laws of war don't reach here. They "can never be applied to citizens in states which have upheld the authority of the government, and where the courts are open and their process unobstructed."
4. Necessity creates the rule and necessity limits it. Martial rule is proper only where courts are actually closed and it is impossible to administer justice — "on the theatre of active military operations, where war really prevails." If it continues after courts are reinstated, "it is a gross usurpation of power." "Martial rule can never exist where the courts are open, and in the proper and unobstructed exercise of their jurisdiction." It is "confined to the locality of actual war" — it could be enforced in Virginia and not in Indiana.
The line that answers the government's necessity argument
The Court asks why Milligan wasn't simply handed to the Circuit Court of Indiana, and answers: no reason of necessity could be urged, since Congress had defined the offenses and directed that court to hear them. Soon after the military tribunal ended, "the Circuit Court met, peacefully transacted its business, and adjourned. It needed no bayonets to protect it."
Its role here
Structurally Bronner's best case: a civilian, where courts are open, pulled into military process. The majority distinguishes it on a single ground — Milligan was not part of or supporting enemy forces. Everything on Question 2 turns on whether that distinction holds, which turns on whether the belligerency label has been tested by anyone.
287 U.S. 341 (1932)In your files

Costanzo v. Tillinghast — a grammar fight about a deportation statute

What happened
An Italian national was ordered deported under § 19 of the Immigration Act of 1917 for managing a house of prostitution, more than five years after entering. Section 19 was a single sentence of nearly nine hundred words, with eleven subject-clauses and five provisos. He argued the opening clause's "within five years after entry" carried over to his clause.
Held
It did not. Deportation on this ground may occur at any time after entry.
The reasoning
Three of the eleven following clauses had their own time references and seven had none, so the five-year limit plainly did not carry to all of them. Punctuation is not decisive of statutory construction, and "we should not apply the rules of syntax to defeat the evident legislative intent." A third proviso, applying the section "irrespective of the time of their entry," would have nothing to operate on under the petitioner's reading. Legislative history confirmed it.
The acquiescence passage — the reason this case is in the file at all
At the very end, as a makeweight: the Bureau of Immigration's rules, adopted in 1917 and carried forward through seven successive editions plus later rules in 1924 and 1925, uniformly held no time limitation applied. "The failure of Congress to alter or amend the section, notwithstanding this consistent construction by the department charged with its enforcement, creates a presumption in favor of the administrative interpretation, to which we should give great weight, even if we doubted the correctness of the ruling."
What it actually establishes
A canon of statutory construction about agency interpretations of the agency's own enabling statute, requiring a consistent and published construction over a long period. That is a narrow thing.
Its role here and its limits
The majority uses it for the proposition that legislative inaction can create a presumption of congressional acquiescence in executive practice, conceding that "Costanzo involved immigration administration" but asserting the principle "equally applies."
It is the weakest authority in the government's chain, for three reasons: it concerns an agency reading its own statute, not a President claiming constitutional power; the practice here is contested rather than consistent; and congressional inaction in this record runs in both directions — Congress failed to pass bills forbidding the power and failed to pass bills granting it.
299 U.S. 304 (1936)In your files

United States v. Curtiss-Wright Export Corp. — machine guns to Bolivia

What happened
Congress passed a joint resolution authorizing the President to prohibit arms sales to countries fighting in the Chaco War if he found it would help restore peace. Roosevelt issued the proclamation. Curtiss-Wright, indicted for conspiring to sell fifteen machine guns to Bolivia, argued the resolution was an unconstitutional delegation of legislative power.
Held
The delegation was valid.
The reasoning
Sutherland distinguished internal from external affairs. Powers over foreign relations did not come from the States by enumeration but passed to the national government as incidents of sovereignty. Strict non-delegation limits applicable to domestic legislation therefore do not apply the same way abroad. Along the way he described the President as the "sole organ of the federal government in the field of international relations," and noted that the wisdom of requiring narrow standards is doubtful where the President's action may depend on confidential information or on effects on foreign relations.
What it establishes — and what it does not
It establishes that Congress may delegate more broadly in foreign affairs. It does not establish unilateral presidential power, and you have Jackson's own words for that: he wrote in Youngstown footnote 2 that Curtiss-Wright "involved, not the question of the President's power to act without congressional authority, but the question of his right to act under and in accord with an Act of Congress"; that "much of the Court's opinion is dictum"; and that while it intimated the President might act in external affairs without congressional authority, it did "not [intimate] that he might act contrary to an Act of Congress."
Its role here
The majority cites it for "plenary and exclusive" power as "sole organ." Jackson's footnote is the complete answer, and it comes from a case the majority itself relies on.
317 U.S. 1 (1942)In your files

Ex parte Quirin — eight men off a U-boat

What happened
In June 1942, eight German-trained saboteurs landed from submarines in darkness — four on Long Island, four at Ponte Vedra Beach, Florida. They carried explosives, buried their German uniforms, changed into civilian clothes, and set out to destroy American war industries. All had lived in the United States; all but one were admittedly German citizens. Herbert Haupt was a U.S. citizen. Roosevelt appointed a military commission by proclamation. They were tried; six were executed.
Held
The military commission was lawfully constituted and the petitioners were properly triable before it.
The reasoning
The law of war distinguishes lawful from unlawful belligerents. Lawful belligerents — uniformed forces — may be captured and held as prisoners of war. Unlawful belligerents — those who pass secretly through the lines in civilian dress to wage war by destruction of life or property — are additionally subject to trial and punishment by military tribunals for acts that render their belligerency unlawful.
On citizenship: "citizenship in the United States of an enemy belligerent does not relieve him from the consequences of a belligerency which is unlawful." The Court assumed Haupt's citizenship and held it made no difference.
How Quirin handled Milligan
It did not overrule it. It distinguished it: Milligan was a non-belligerent, a resident of a state that had upheld federal authority, not part of or associated with the armed forces of the enemy. Quirin's petitioners had admitted facts placing them squarely in the enemy-belligerent category.
Its role here — and the distinction that actually matters
The government's strongest case, because it defeats two intuitive arguments at once: arrest on U.S. soil doesn't matter, and citizenship doesn't matter.
But note what was not in dispute in Quirin: belligerency itself. The petitioners admitted arriving from an enemy submarine, in the uniform of a nation with which the United States was at a declared war, carrying explosives. Quirin answers the question what may be done to a belligerent. It does not answer who decides whether someone is one — which is the only question actually contested in Bronner's case.
343 U.S. 579 (1952)In your files

Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer — the steel mills Truman couldn't keep

What happened
During the Korean War, a nationwide steel strike threatened war production. Truman ordered the Secretary of Commerce to seize and operate the mills. He reported to Congress twice; Congress did nothing. Congress had considered and rejected giving presidents seizure authority when it passed the Taft-Hartley Act in 1947, and had provided three other statutory mechanisms for comparable situations, none of which Truman used.
Held
Unconstitutional. 6–3.
The majority (Black)
Short and formal. Presidential power must stem either from an act of Congress or from the Constitution itself. No statute authorized the seizure. The Commander in Chief clause does not extend to taking possession of private property to settle a labor dispute in a domestic industry — "this is a job for the Nation's lawmakers, not for its military authorities."
Jackson's concurrence
The three categories, and the reasoning behind them. See the framework section — it is important enough to have its own treatment.
What it establishes
The organizing framework for every subsequent separation-of-powers dispute, and the specific principle that where Congress has legislated in a field and declined to confer the power the executive claims, courts scrutinize that claim with caution.
Its role here
The battlefield. The majority places the President in Category 1; the dissent says Category 3, "at best" Category 2. The majority also cites it for the proposition — which nobody disputes — that no granted power may be exercised in a way that deprives individuals of constitutional rights.
424 U.S. 319 (1976)In your files

Mathews v. Eldridge — disability benefits, cut off without a hearing

What happened
George Eldridge received Social Security disability benefits. A state agency reviewed his file, sent him a questionnaire, obtained reports from his physician and a psychiatric consultant, and tentatively concluded his disability had ended. He was given a summary of the evidence and an opportunity to respond in writing. Benefits were terminated. He was entitled to a full evidentiary hearing afterward, with retroactive relief if he won.
Held
An evidentiary hearing is not required before termination. The existing procedures satisfied due process.
The test it created
"[I]dentification of the specific dictates of due process generally requires consideration of three distinct factors:"
First, the private interest that will be affected by the official action. Second, the risk of an erroneous deprivation through the procedures used, and the probable value, if any, of additional or substitute safeguards. Third, the government's interest, including the function involved and the fiscal and administrative burdens the additional procedure would entail.
What to notice about it
Two things. It is a balancing test, so it rarely produces bright lines. And it was created in a case where the claimant lost — the Court found that disability determinations turn on relatively objective medical evidence, reducing error risk, and that the recipient wasn't in the same desperate position as the welfare recipient in Goldberg v. Kelly. Mathews is not a plaintiff-friendly test by design.
Its role here
Both opinions apply it, via Hamdi. Everything depends on factor one — Hamdi says freedom from physical restraint is "the most elemental of liberty interests" — and on whether the government's asserted burden (disclosure would compromise national security) is treated as an ordinary administrative cost or as something categorically different.
542 U.S. 507 (2004)In your files

Hamdi v. Rumsfeld — the American captured in Afghanistan

What happened
Yaser Hamdi, born in Louisiana and raised in Saudi Arabia, was seized in Afghanistan by the Northern Alliance and turned over to the U.S. military, which alleged he was a Taliban fighter. He was taken to Guantanamo; when his American citizenship was discovered he was moved to a naval brig in Virginia. He was held without charge, without counsel, and without any hearing. The government's entire evidentiary submission was a short declaration from a Defense Department official — the "Mobbs Declaration."
Held — split two ways
On authority: the Authorization for Use of Military Force (AUMF) authorized his detention. Detention of enemy combatants for the duration of the relevant conflict is a "fundamental incident of waging war" and therefore falls within "necessary and appropriate force."
On process: a citizen-detainee seeking to challenge his classification must receive notice of the factual basis for that classification and a fair opportunity to rebut the government's assertions before a neutral decisionmaker.
The accommodations the plurality allowed
It is not an ordinary criminal trial. Hearsay may be accepted. A rebuttable presumption may be applied in favor of the government's evidence, so long as the detainee has a fair chance to rebut it. The plurality suggested a properly constituted military tribunal could satisfy the requirement.
The line everyone quotes
"[A] state of war is not a blank check for the President when it comes to the rights of the Nation's citizens."
How the Justices divided
O'Connor announced the judgment; her opinion is a plurality of four (with Rehnquist, Kennedy, Breyer). Souter, joined by Ginsburg, concurred in part and dissented in part — they thought the detention was not authorized at all under the Non-Detention Act, but joined to give Hamdi a remand. Scalia, joined by Stevens, dissented: a citizen must be charged with treason or another crime, or Congress must suspend habeas — no third option. Thomas dissented the other way: the detention was a valid exercise of war powers and the plurality gave insufficient deference.
So: eight Justices agreed Hamdi could not be held on the process he received, for two incompatible reasons. Lower courts treat the plurality's process holding as controlling.
Its role here
The template for the likely outcome and the case both sides need. Note the two structural distinctions the government presses: Hamdi was a citizen, and he was captured in an active combat zone. Bronner is neither.
115 F.4th 928 (8th Cir. 2024)Not in your files

Banyee v. Garland — the circuit case both sides claim

What it addresses
Prolonged immigration detention and when due process requires additional procedure. Not binding on the Supreme Court, and the only source for it in your materials is how the two opinions below characterize it.
How the majority uses it
Courts have not categorically banned detentions longer than six months, nor held that detainees are entitled to an "individual determination" of each detention decision — especially absent evidence the detention is a "ruse to incarcerate [him] for other reasons."
How the dissent uses it
Even where statutes authorize detention, due process may require periodic review to prevent detention from becoming effectively indefinite. The dissent presents it as proof that courts can craft procedures protecting security and liberty at once.
Why it matters
It is the only place in the record where a concrete remedy short of release is described. Any judge looking for a way to rule for Bronner without dismantling war powers will reach for periodic review, and this is where it comes from.

title: Applied to Bronner
html:
Applied to Bronner — what each fact does

The first column concerns statutory fit, civilian process, and error risk. The second concerns the alleged threat, war powers, and congressional language. Hamdi leaves room for detention authority while requiring more process.

Pushes toward "exceeded his authority"
  • Thirty years of continuous lawful residence; entered at fifteen as an asylee. R. 4
  • Naturalization approved Feb 17, 2025, with an express good moral character finding. Oath scheduled July 4; military transfer July 7. R. 4, 8
  • No prior convictions. The AG classified him as having a "criminal record" because he had been accused. R. 8
  • Arraigned in an Article III court, pled not guilty, released on bond — the exact Milligan situation, and evidence that the error risk under Mathews factor two is not hypothetical. R. 8; dissent R. 19
  • Twelve months in military custody, uncharged, on sealed evidence he has never seen. R. 7–8
  • Anti-Terrorist Act (ATA) § 4 supplies no time limit, no dangerousness finding, no counsel, no judicial review. R. 3; App. V (R. 24)
  • ATA § 4(b)(1) permits offshore detention only for the unlawfully present; § 4(b)(2) requires citizens be held inside. Bronner falls in neither. R. 3; App. V (R. 24)
  • A 2026 House bill to authorize offshore detention of lawfully present non-citizens is still pending in the Senate — Congress is presently deciding whether to grant the power the President claims he already has. R. 3
  • National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) § 1021(b)(2) requires a connection to al-Qaeda, the Taliban, or associated forces. The record says the sellers were questioned about suspected ties to organizations involved in drug smuggling. That is several inferential steps short of the statutory element, and it concerns them, not him. R. 7; App. III (R. 21)
  • The President's signing-ceremony statement that inherent powers allow him to act "beyond any specific law or statutory framework." R. 3–4
Pushes toward "within his authority"
  • Sealed warehouse documents the government says show an arranged purchase of a radiological weapon. R. 7–8
  • Roper and Langbourne: foreign convictions for selling military-grade arms; questioned twice by federal agents about terrorist ties. R. 7
  • Fentanyl patches, lollipops, spray, a sales log, four boxes of lozenges in the car — the drug case is strong on its own. R. 7
  • Independent NSA surveillance separately observed the warehouse meeting. R. 7
  • NDAA § 1021(a) affirms detention authority; § 1021(c)(1) expressly permits detention without trial until hostilities end. This is affirmative statutory text and it is the government's best card. App. III (R. 21); R. 13
  • § 1022(b) exempts citizens and lawful residents from the requirement of military custody — arguably lifting an obligation, not a power. App. IV (R. 22); R. 2
  • § 1021(d) and (e) and ATA § 4(c): nothing limits or expands existing authority — which keeps the field open and argues against Category 3. R. 21, 24; discussed R. 2–3, 14
  • 10 U.S.C. § 948(a)(7)(B) covers those who purposefully and materially support hostilities. App. II (R. 20); R. 12
  • Senate efforts to bar indefinite detention failed repeatedly; Authorization for Use of Military Force (AUMF) repeal failed in 2023 and 2025; a signing statement asserted the power and Congress did not respond. R. 3
  • Quirin: neither citizenship nor arrest on U.S. soil is disqualifying. R. 12
  • Habeas is functioning — he filed, won below, and is before the Supreme Court. R. 8–9, 14
  • Government states it intends to try him as soon as practicable; delay is attributed to evidence sensitivity, not punishment. R. 8, 14
Authority, process, and uncertainty

Hamdi supports a possible split result: the authority argument is winnable for the government and the process argument is winnable for Bronner. Hamdi split exactly that way — the AUMF authorized detention, and the process Hamdi received was constitutionally insufficient.

Two distinctions decide whether Hamdi transfers. Citizenship: Hamdi's process holding is framed for "a citizen-detainee," but the Fifth Amendment's word is "person," and lawful permanent residents within the United States have long been held to have due process rights. Capture location: Hamdi was seized in an active combat zone where belligerency was evidenced by circumstance; Bronner was arrested at home by civilian police and arraigned. That second distinction cuts toward more process, not less — the further you get from a battlefield, the weaker the case for battlefield rules.

The two record wrinkles on Question 2

1. Section numbering. Page 3 of the record attributes the "nothing shall be construed to affect existing law" language to § 1022(e); the dissent attributes it to § 1021(e); Appendix III shows it at § 1021(e). Appendix IV (§ 1022) has no subsection (e) at all. Cite Appendix III.

2. The AG's stated reason. He classified Bronner as a non-citizen "with a criminal record" because he had been "accused." That is a misuse of the term. But EO 15,000 covers non-citizens with criminal records or pending criminal charges, and Bronner had pending charges. The order's terms are arguably satisfied even though the AG's stated reason is wrong. Both sides should know which of those they're talking about.

title: The hinge
html:
How Question 1 affects Question 2

The two questions are legally distinct, but the stipulated chain of evidence connects the camera surveillance to the government's belligerency classification.

Bronner argues that an unlawful search undermines the evidence supporting military classification. The government argues that suppression and detention authority are separate questions. The supplied cases do not fully resolve that interaction.

  1. The parties stipulate that the government relied primarily on the pole-camera footage to establish probable cause for the warrants.
  2. Footnote 8: the government did not assert it had probable cause without that footage. That is a waiver.
  3. The warrants produced the search of the warehouse.
  4. The warehouse produced the sealed documents.
  5. The sealed documents are the only basis for calling Bronner an unprivileged enemy belligerent — the fentanyl is drug evidence, not terrorism evidence.

If the exclusionary rule removes the warehouse documents after an unlawful camera search, the record may lose its only stated basis for treating Bronner as a belligerent rather than an ordinary criminal defendant.

Why this helps Bronner
  • It converts Question 2 from a war-powers abstraction into a question about the reliability of an executive determination — which is Mathews factor two.
  • It raises the stakes on Question 1: this is not a suppression motion about fentanyl, it is the origin of a twelve-month detention.
  • Footnote 8 forecloses the independent source exception, which is normally the government's escape from fruit-of-the-poisonous-tree.
The government's answers, and their weaknesses
  • Separate the questions. The government argues that Article II concerns legal authority to detain, while suppression concerns the evidence in the criminal case. Whether suppression doctrine carries into this habeas challenge is genuinely uncertain on the authorities provided.
  • Point to the NSA. Agents Bourgeois and Quinlan observed the warehouse meeting independently. Weakness: they declined to disclose their purpose or intelligence, so by definition none of it is in the record. You cannot build an independent-source argument from something nobody would describe.
  • Note what remains. Even without the documents, the fentanyl evidence supports an ordinary prosecution. Weakness: that is precisely Bronner's point — an ordinary prosecution is what an Article III court had already begun.

title: Glossary & acronyms
html:
Glossary & acronyms

Use this as a reference while you read the record and the two questions. The first group identifies the laws, institutions, and citation labels in the problem. The later groups explain the legal terms and show why each one matters to Bronner.

Acronyms and governing documents

AUMF
Authorization for Use of Military Force. Congress enacted this law after September 11, 2001. It authorizes the President to use necessary and appropriate force against the people, organizations, and nations responsible for those attacks, or those who harbored them. In Bronner, the government treats the AUMF as one source of detention authority. Bronner argues that the alleged dirty-bomb transaction has not been tied to al-Qaeda, the Taliban, or an associated force. App. I (R. 20)
NDAA
National Defense Authorization Act. The relevant law is the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2012. Section 1021 describes who may count as a covered person and confirms law-of-war detention authority. Section 1022 addresses mandatory military custody and excludes citizens and some lawful permanent residents from that requirement. The parties disagree about whether those exclusions remove only a duty to detain or also limit the power to detain. App. III–IV (R. 21–22)
ATA
Anti-Terrorist Act. This is a fictional federal statute enacted for the Bronner problem. It authorizes detention of people suspected of terrorism and gives express offshore-detention rules for unlawfully present non-citizens and citizens. It does not give an express rule for lawfully present non-citizens such as Bronner. That gap drives the dispute over what Congress authorized. App. V (R. 23–24)
PAT
Protection Against Terrorism. This is the fictional short name for Executive Order 15,000 in the moot record. It is not the PATRIOT Act. President DeNolf used PAT to direct the offshore detention of certain non-citizens with criminal records or pending criminal charges. Bronner had a pending charge but no conviction. App. VI (R. 25)
EO
Executive order. A written presidential directive to the executive branch. It is not an Act of Congress and cannot create authority that the Constitution and statutes deny. The relevant order is EO 15,000, also called PAT.
AG
Attorney General. The head of the Department of Justice. Attorney General Chester Comerford applied PAT and the ATA to Bronner and classified him for offshore detention. R. 8
DOJ
Department of Justice. The executive department responsible for federal law enforcement and prosecution. The ATA directs the Attorney General to use DOJ detention authority.
FBI
Federal Bureau of Investigation. The federal law-enforcement agency whose agents installed the pole cameras, investigated Bronner, and obtained the evidence used in the criminal case.
NSA
National Security Agency. The intelligence agency whose agents separately observed the warehouse meeting. The record does not disclose why they were watching. R. 7
AUSA
Assistant United States Attorney. A federal prosecutor. AUSA Amanda DeLeon prepared the warrant applications after receiving information from Agent Cruz. R. 7
USCIS
United States Citizenship and Immigration Services. The agency that approved Bronner's naturalization after finding that he met the statutory requirements, including good moral character. He had not yet taken the oath, so he was still a lawful permanent resident rather than a citizen. R. 4
AMCA
American Moot Court Association. The organization associated with this moot problem. The record's cover page contains its attribution note.
CSLI
Cell-site location information. A phone company creates these records when a phone connects to cell towers. The records can reveal where a person traveled over time. Carpenter held that obtaining at least seven days of historical CSLI is a Fourth Amendment search. Bronner's case involves cameras rather than CSLI, but the dissent uses Carpenter's concern with long-term aggregation.
GTMO / Guantanamo
Guantanamo Bay. The United States naval base in Cuba where Bronner is held in military custody. Calling it “offshore” matters because the ATA treats detention inside and outside the territorial United States differently.
R.
Record. A citation such as R. 7 points to a page in the moot-court record. This guide uses PDF page numbers. The record map explains the one-page difference between PDF and printed numbering.
App.
Appendix. The record appendices reproduce the AUMF, the statutory definition of unprivileged enemy belligerent, NDAA §§ 1021–1022, the ATA, and EO 15,000.
P.L.
Public Law. The number assigned to a federal law when Congress enacts it. For example, the NDAA in this problem is Public Law 112-81.
U.S.C.
United States Code. The organized compilation of federal statutes. A citation such as 10 U.S.C. § 948a(7) identifies the title, code, and section.

Fourth Amendment terms

Search
A Fourth Amendment search can occur without touching property or entering a home. Under Katz, the question is whether the government intruded on an expectation of privacy that society recognizes as reasonable. Bronner argues that 93 days of targeted recording exposed a private pattern of life. The government answers that each camera recorded only what a passerby could see from public property.
Reasonable expectation of privacy
The Katz test has two parts. First, the person must have treated the matter as private. Second, society must be prepared to recognize that expectation as reasonable. The second part is the contested one here because parts of Bronner's porch, steps, driveway, and windows were visible from the street.
Curtilage
The area immediately surrounding a home, such as a porch or enclosed yard. The law treats curtilage as closely connected to the home. The cameras did not physically enter Bronner's property, but they continuously recorded activity around it.
Sense-enhancing technology not in general public use
Kyllo uses this phrase for technology that lets the government learn details about the interior of a home that ordinary observation could not reveal. The government says Ring cameras are common consumer devices. Bronner argues that four cameras used together for 93 days produced surveillance no ordinary passerby could replicate.
Mosaic theory / aggregation
The idea that many lawful observations can reveal protected information when the government combines them over time. A single delivery may say little. Months of deliveries, visitors, lights, and routines can describe a household's pattern of life. No Supreme Court majority has adopted the “mosaic theory” by name, and Tuggle says lower courts are not required to apply it. The dissent nevertheless reads Carpenter as supporting the underlying concern.
Third-party doctrine
The rule that information voluntarily given to another person or company often receives less Fourth Amendment protection. Carpenter declined to apply that rule mechanically to historical CSLI because carrying a phone is nearly unavoidable and the records reveal extensive location history.
Fruit of the poisonous tree
Evidence discovered because of an unconstitutional search may also be excluded. Three doctrines can break that connection. An independent source means police obtained the evidence through a separate lawful route. Inevitable discovery means they would have found it lawfully anyway. Attenuation means the connection became too remote. The problem limits these routes because the parties stipulated that the government relied primarily on the camera footage.
Good-faith exception
Courts may admit evidence when officers reasonably relied on a facially valid warrant or on binding precedent that later changes. In Moore-Bush, this exception controlled the result even though several judges believed the surveillance was a search. Bronner's problem instead asks directly whether the surveillance was a search.
Exigency / exigent circumstances
An emergency that makes waiting for a warrant impracticable, such as an immediate threat to life or imminent destruction of evidence. The dissent stresses that agents watched for weeks and could reach a magistrate at night, so the record does not show that an emergency prevented them from seeking a warrant.

Article II and detention terms

Youngstown categories
Justice Jackson's framework measures presidential authority by asking what Congress has done. In Category 1, Congress authorized the act and presidential power is strongest. In Category 2, Congress has not resolved the issue and the President may rely on independent authority. In Category 3, the President acts against Congress's express or implied position and must show that the Constitution gives him exclusive control. The government places Bronner in Category 1. Bronner argues for Category 3, or at least Category 2.
Zone of twilight
Jackson's name for Category 2. Congress has neither clearly authorized nor clearly forbidden the presidential act, or both branches may possess overlapping authority. It is a description of the relationship between Congress and the President, not a separate source of power.
Lowest ebb
Jackson's name for Category 3. The President acts against Congress's express or implied will, so his claim is weakest. The act survives only if the Constitution gives the President exclusive power over the subject and therefore prevents Congress from controlling it.
Unprivileged enemy belligerent
A statutory classification under 10 U.S.C. § 948a(7). It can include someone who engaged in hostilities, purposefully and materially supported hostilities, belonged to al-Qaeda at the relevant time, or had previously been classified as an enemy combatant. The label matters because it can support military detention or trial. The dispute is not merely whether the Attorney General used the label. It is whether the facts and governing statutes legally place Bronner within it. App. II (R. 20)
Covered person
A person within NDAA § 1021(b). The definition covers people responsible for September 11 and those who were part of or substantially supported al-Qaeda, the Taliban, or associated forces engaged in hostilities against the United States. The government says Bronner's alleged conduct places him within that authority. Bronner argues that the record does not connect him to any listed or associated force. App. III (R. 21)
Material support
Purposeful and meaningful assistance to prohibited hostilities or to a designated foreign terrorist organization, depending on the statute being applied. The government treats the alleged effort to obtain dirty-bomb material as support. Bronner denies reviewing the sealed documents and argues that suspicion of terrorism is not the same as support for al-Qaeda, the Taliban, or an associated force.
Enemy combatant
An older classification for a person treated as fighting for or supporting an enemy. The statutory definition of unprivileged enemy belligerent includes a person previously determined to be an enemy combatant. A classification cannot answer the separate question whether the President had legal authority to detain this person. App. II (R. 20)
Lawful and unlawful belligerents
Quirin distinguishes fighters who comply with the law of war from those who do not. Lawful combatants may be held as prisoners of war. Unlawful belligerents may also face military trial and punishment for violating the law of war. Bronner argues that he was a civilian living in the United States, not a fighter captured in a combat zone.
Law-of-war detention
Holding an enemy fighter to prevent a return to battle until the relevant hostilities end. The government characterizes it as prevention rather than criminal punishment, which is why a criminal trial is not always required. Bronner answers that he was removed from an ordinary prosecution and that a conflict with no clear endpoint could turn preventive detention into permanent imprisonment.
Lawful permanent resident
A non-citizen authorized to live permanently in the United States, commonly called a green-card holder. Bronner had held this status since 2010, and USCIS had approved his naturalization. He did not become a citizen because he was detained before taking the oath. R. 4
Habeas corpus
A court proceeding that requires the government to justify a person's detention. It tests the legal basis for confinement rather than deciding the underlying criminal charge. Bronner uses habeas because he remains in military custody without a military trial.
Military commission
A military tribunal used to try offenses against the law of war. It differs from an Article III court, where civilian federal judges exercise the judicial power. Bronner has not been tried by either system on the detention theory. He was arraigned in federal court, released on bond, and then transferred to military custody.
Congressional acquiescence
An argument that Congress accepted an executive interpretation by leaving a longstanding and consistent practice unchanged. Silence alone is not enough. The government relies on failed amendments and repeal efforts. Bronner argues that those events point in different directions and do not amount to affirmative authorization.
“Sole organ”
A phrase from Curtiss-Wright describing the President's role in communicating for the United States in foreign affairs. It does not mean that the President possesses all federal power abroad. Justice Jackson's Youngstown concurrence calls the broader discussion dictum because Curtiss-Wright involved action authorized by Congress.
Dictum
Language in a judicial opinion that was not necessary to decide the case. Dictum may persuade later courts but does not bind them as a holding does. Bronner uses this distinction to narrow Curtiss-Wright's broad statements about presidential foreign-affairs power.
Signing statement
A President's written explanation or objection when signing legislation. It records the executive branch's position but is not itself a statute. The problem uses a prior signing statement as evidence of how the executive branch understood detention authority.
Nondelegation
The constitutional principle that Congress cannot transfer unlimited legislative power to the executive. Curtiss-Wright addressed whether Congress had delegated too broadly. It did not decide whether the President could act without congressional authorization.

Procedure and opinions

Article III court
An ordinary federal court whose judges exercise the judicial power described in Article III and generally hold life tenure. Bronner was arraigned in this civilian system before the executive transferred him to military custody.
Due process
The Fifth Amendment prevents the federal government from depriving a person of life, liberty, or property without lawful procedure. At minimum, Hamdi required notice of the factual basis for detention and a fair opportunity to answer before a neutral decision-maker. The Amendment protects “persons,” not only citizens.
Mathews balancing
The framework from Mathews v. Eldridge asks three questions. What private interest is at stake? How likely is the current process to produce an error, and how much would added safeguards help? What interest and administrative burden does the government face? In Bronner, the private interest is freedom from prolonged military detention, while the government invokes national security and sensitive evidence.
Writ
A formal court order. Granting a writ of habeas corpus means the court has found that the government must justify, alter, or end the detention according to law.
De novo review
Fresh review of a legal question without deferring to the lower court's answer. The parties stipulated the facts, so the appellate dispute concerns what the Constitution and statutes mean.
Stipulated
Agreed by both parties for purposes of the case. A stipulated fact is not open to factual dispute in the argument. That is why the guide uses the record's repeated statement of 93 days even though the dates produce different arithmetic.
Preserved / not preserved
A preserved argument was raised properly and remains available on appeal. An unpreserved argument ordinarily cannot be introduced later. Footnotes 8 and 9 remove several possible claims from this problem, including independent probable cause, the warrant's sufficiency, speedy trial, bail, and international-law arguments.
Waiver
The loss or intentional surrender of a right or argument. A party can waive an issue expressly or by failing to raise it when required.
Holding
The legal rule necessary to reach a court's judgment. Later courts must follow a controlling holding even if they disregard broader commentary in the opinion.
Majority opinion
An opinion whose reasoning receives enough votes to speak for the court. Justice Black wrote the Youngstown majority, while Justice Jackson wrote the separate concurrence that later courts use as the presidential-power framework.
Plurality
The largest group of justices agreeing on a rationale when no rationale receives five votes. Justice O'Connor's Hamdi opinion on process was a four-justice plurality, so its reasoning must be read with the other opinions.
Concurrence in the judgment
An opinion agreeing with the result but not necessarily the majority's reasoning. Justice Jackson concurred in Youngstown's judgment and supplied the three-category framework now used by courts.
Per curiam
An opinion issued in the court's name rather than signed by one judge. The short en banc judgment in Moore-Bush was per curiam because no single rationale commanded a majority.
En banc
Review by all active judges of a federal circuit, rather than the usual three-judge panel. Granting en banc review vacates the panel opinion. In Moore-Bush, the full First Circuit divided over whether the cameras conducted a search.
Certiorari
The Supreme Court's discretionary decision to hear a case. A grant means the Court will review the questions presented; it does not predict which side will win.

title: Corrections & gaps
html:
Corrections and remaining gaps

This section separates corrections to earlier guide language from authorities that are not included in the supplied files. It does not change the stipulated record or either court's holdings.

The Moore-Bush correction changes how that case should be described, not its relevance. Missing authorities can inform preparation only if competition rules permit outside sources.

Correction to the earlier version of this guide

I described Moore-Bush as a 3–3 split that left the district court affirmed by an equally divided court. That is wrong. The en banc First Circuit issued a per curiam judgment unanimously reversing the suppression order. The 3–3 division is over the reasoning: Barron, Thompson, and Kayatta held it was a search but reversed on the good-faith exception (because circuit precedent, Bucci, had said otherwise); Lynch, Howard, and Gelpí held it was not a search.

Practical consequence: the case is not authority that pole-camera surveillance requires suppression. It is authority that the constitutional question divides serious judges evenly — and that even a court finding a search may decline to suppress.

The Eighth Amendment label

You originally described these as the Eighth Amendment table of authorities. There is no Eighth Amendment issue in this case — no cruel-and-unusual-punishment question, no sentencing question. Q1 is Fourth Amendment; Q2 is Article II plus Fifth Amendment due process.

Still not in your files

The supplied files include every case cited by the two opinions except the following authorities.

  • Banyee v. Garland, 115 F.4th 928 (8th Cir. 2024) — cited by both opinions for opposite propositions. The only source of the periodic-review remedy.
  • United States v. Bucci, 582 F.3d 108 (1st Cir. 2009) — the precedent Moore-Bush was about overruling, and the source of the "no fences, gates, or shrubbery" reasoning the government's brief will echo.
  • United States v. Houston, 813 F.3d 282 (6th Cir. 2016) — the source of the "possibility, not practicability" fiction that Tuggle rejected and the trial court in Tafoya relied on.
  • United States v. Knotts, 460 U.S. 276 (1983) — the "augment the sensory faculties bestowed upon them at birth" line.
  • State v. Jones, 903 N.W.2d 101 (S.D. 2017) — two months of pole-camera surveillance of street-visible activities held to be a search. On the split table above, this is the single most useful non-binding case for Bronner, because it is the only one finding a search without a fence doing the work.

Worth reading if your rules permit citing outside the case file: Boumediene v. Bush, 553 U.S. 723 (2008) (habeas extends to Guantanamo — though jurisdiction is stipulated here) and Zivotofsky v. Kerry, 576 U.S. 1 (2015) (rejecting the "sole organ" reading of Curtiss-Wright). Check the AMCA rules first.
